papers.title: Numerical Implementation of Just-In-Time Decoding in Novel Lattice Slices Through the Three-Dimensional Surface Code

genuine.note: Cited for d^3 spacetime scaling of constant-time universal operations in the 3D surface code, but the cited work states that a 3D surface code needs an unknown number of syndrome-extraction rounds and that single-shot decoding of its string-like Z errors seems unlikely; d^3 is established there only for 3D gauge colour codes.

false_alarm.note: Brown's paper performs a controlled-controlled-phase gate with three overlapping 2D surface codes over a time that scales with system size, using a just-in-time decoder, and proves a threshold; the sentence is accurate.
The citation credits the term 'dimension jumping' to Bombín's dimensional-jump paper; the surface-code version is Brown's, as the next sentence of the citing paper says.

The cited work assigns the three codes' string-like logical operators to the x, y and z axes of the rectified lattice, i.e. they are perpendicular; the word itself does not appear, which is all the judge objected to.

The text the current pipeline read gives a threshold lower bound of ε ∼ 10^-17, matching the claim; the number-drift tag is a parsing error (PDF text '10−17' read as the number 10). The old pipeline read a different version giving 6·10^-15 and called it contradicted (version mismatch).
The cited work does report a 4D toric code with a transversal CCCZ; the flagged part ('it seems natural to ask if an equivalent process could be used...') is the citing authors' own open question.

Unfolding the color code shows a transversal d-qubit control-Z on a stack of d copies of the d-dimensional toric code, i.e. CCCZ for d = 4; that is a result regarding transversal CCCZ in the 4D surface code.

debatable.note: Group citation [5, 23, 24] for the 3D colour code: [5] introduces colour codes (in 2D only); the 3D colour code is in [23, 24]. A fair pointer to the code family, loosely placed.

Bombín does note the dimensional puzzle (constant-time universal operations in 3D, not in 2D), which is the qualitative point; the O(d^3)/O(d^4) spacetime costs and O(d) rounds are the citing authors' own elaboration and are not in the cited text.

papers.title: Small Planets Around Cool Dwarfs: Enhanced Formation Efficiency of Super-Earths around M dwarfs

false_alarm.note: 'As inferred from': Birnstiel et al. tabulate exponents of n(m)·m·a of 1/2 (turbulent) and 1/4 (settling), which per unit Stokes number give exactly St^-0.5 and St^-0.75. The current judge did not do the conversion; the old pipeline could not see the table.
The source gives the dust sublimation temperature as ≈1800-2000 K, the thermostat behind the 2000 K cap; the number-drift tag compares 2000 with the lower end of the range (both pipelines).
Method citation for the self-similar viscous disk solution (Σ ∝ 1/ν in the inner disk), which Lynden-Bell & Pringle introduced; the pressure scaling is the citing authors' derivation.

Lee & Chiang find cores above ~5 Earth masses cannot avoid runaway in gas-rich disks, so a 9-10 Earth-mass core suffices; 'always ≳ 9-10' refers to the citing authors' own isolation mass, not the cited work.
Piso et al. compute a critical core mass of ~8 Earth masses at 5 AU, below the citing authors' isolation mass of 9-10, so the latter suffices; the number-drift tag compares two different quantities.

Venturini et al. give critical masses of ~10 Earth masses, falling with envelope enrichment, which supports both parts of the sentence; the old pipeline's 'contradicted' reads a lower bound on the needed mass as a contradiction.
Chachan et al. show that disks massive enough to build cold-giant cores can deliver enough solids inward to form inner super-Earths; 'in agreement with' is a fair comparison by the citing authors.

Kimura et al. challenge the assumption that icy aggregates have much higher disruption velocities than silicate ones, i.e. fragmentation velocities are more uniform than assumed; the term v_f is the citing paper's.
Musiolik & Wurm find water ice has no sticking advantage over silicates at the measured temperatures, supporting a more uniform fragmentation velocity.
Dressing & Charbonneau report higher small-planet occurrence around M dwarfs than FGK stars (0.83 per M dwarf HZ vs 22%), the observed enhancement the sentence refers to.
Joint citation: Dawson et al. simulate the giant-impact phase that grows embryos into super-Earths, Lee & Chiang the final mass doubling; each supports its part.
Lee & Chiang describe the final doubling of core mass by mergers of protocores in the gas-depleted late stage, i.e. giant impacts.
Manara et al. convert fluxes to dust masses with this opacity and T = 20 K under the optically thin assumption, as the sentence says.
Data-source citation: the VANDAM survey measured Class I disk dust masses in Orion with the VLA; 'better mass estimates' was the judge's own reading of the context.
Data-source citation: the citing authors ran the regression on Tobin et al.'s Class I VLA data; the exponent 0.25 is their result, not one claimed for the cited paper.

'The relation we get for the Manara et al. sample': the citing authors fit the compiled data themselves; the different slopes Manara et al. quote for individual regions do not make this a citation problem.
β_M ~ 1 is the citing authors' own fit to the Manara et al. compilation (previous sentence), not a value claimed for the cited paper.
β_T = 0.125 or 0.5 are the citing authors' limiting cases derived in the previous sentences for the Tobin et al. sample, not values claimed for the cited paper.

The source says at least 10 Earth masses are lost to drift for every 1 Earth mass netted, so a ~10 Earth-mass isolation core implies ~100 Earth masses drifted; 10 AU is the citing authors' example location.

debatable.note: Group citation (e.g., four occurrence-rate studies) for a summary range: this work finds ~3.8 times more small habitable-zone planets around M dwarfs than FGK stars (inside the 3-10 range); the 50-100 day window and super-Earth/mini-Neptune size range are the citing authors' synthesis.

Group citation (e.g., four occurrence-rate studies) for a summary range: this work reports elevated Earth- to Neptune-size planet occurrence around M dwarfs without a factor; a fair member of the group, but it does not give the 3-10 factor.

Group citation (e.g., four occurrence-rate studies) for a summary range: this work finds M-dwarf rates elevated relative to FGK (factors of a few for 2-32 days); the 50-100 day window is the citing authors' extension.
Group citation (e.g., four occurrence-rate studies) for a summary range: this work gives factors of 2 (vs G) to 3 (vs F) up to 50-day periods, at the low end of or below the cited 3-10 range.

The source finds its preliminary conditional occurrence 'similar to the underlying rate' of field stars; 'statistically consistent' implies a test it does not report. Co-cited with Bonomo et al. (2023).
Manara et al. report Macc-M* slopes of ~1.6-2 (B = 2 is the upper end, not a measured mean); the 30-70 percentile accretion-rate range is the citing authors' reading of the compiled data ('e.g.').

Cited with three other works for runaway masses that depend on opacity and metallicity, which this work discusses; it quotes ~15 Earth-mass cores for giant nucleation, above the citing authors' 9-10, so the agreement is loose.

'In agreement with previous results': Lin et al. show pebble accretion of an outer core drifts large solid masses inward, consistent with the citing result, but they do not state it about inner and outer planets.
The cited work's no-snow-line case appears in its second figure in the text we read, not Figure 1; plot legends are not in the text and journal figure numbering may differ.
CLS II confirms giant-planet occurrence increases with stellar mass and that M dwarfs have lower rates, but gives no factor of 2-3; the factor may come from the co-cited Clanton & Gaudi.
Bonnell et al. introduce competitive accretion; the accretion-rate scaling in the sentence appears to come from McKee & Offner's analytic approximation, cited alongside.

papers.title: Quasi-local studies of the particle surfaces and their stability in general spacetimes

false_alarm.note: The correspondence F = f, H = 1/g matches the cited metric; the remark about a sign difference from metric signature is the citing authors' own comparison.
Claudel et al. give the unit normal of an SO(3)-invariant timelike hypersurface in a general spherically symmetric metric; the citing authors write it in their own f, g notation.

Synge's 1966 paper on photon escape from compact stars is the classic derivation of the escape cone set by the photon sphere, i.e. the shadow boundary; only its abstract was available, and the off-topic tag (both pipelines) is wrong.
As for s28: the general unit-normal formula of [32], specialised by the citing authors to Vaidya coordinates.
'Consistent with the result in [45]': [45] obtains the ISCO evolution in Vaidya spacetime (numerically, shown in a figure); the consistency check is the citing authors'.
The cited work gives the slow-rotation Kerr-Vaidya metric on the equatorial plane, which is what the marker is attached to; the tangent-vector definitions that follow are the citing authors'.

'The result is consistent with [45]': [45] derives ISCO evolution equations in dynamical spherically symmetric spacetimes by another method; the consistency is the citing authors' own comparison (both pipelines too literal).

Claudel, Virbhadra and Ellis introduced the (quasi-local) definition of photon surfaces, which the field credits as the first; the paper not saying 'first' about itself does not make the attribution wrong.

debatable.note: Cederbaum & Jahns treat spherical photon orbits (constant r) in Kerr; extending 'not evolved, r = constant' to general stationary axisymmetric spacetimes goes a little beyond the source. The corrected-source tag (an erratum) is legitimate.

papers.title: Cryptic Zika virus infections unmasked from suspected malaria cases in Northeastern Nigeria

genuine.note: A paper on calculating sample sizes for medical studies is cited for what PRNT measures (antibody quantity and effectiveness); it has nothing on PRNT or antibodies. Probably the wrong reference.
Cited as agreeing with chikungunya in 39% of patients, but the Colombian surveillance study found CHIKV in 1.07% of samples; the 'agreement' does not hold.

The cited narrative review summarises mostly preclinical (in silico, in vitro, animal) antiviral activity of approved antimicrobials; it does not establish them as 'effective treatments for many viral diseases', and it never mentions ivermectin (mefloquine, chloroquine, erythromycin and tetracyclines do appear).

The source reports 2,439 cases of a congenital syndrome associated with Zika; the citing sentence says 'genital syndrome'. The case counts match, so it is a misreport (probably a typo) that changes the meaning.

false_alarm.note: The cited study uses PRNT90 as a confirmatory test to rule out dengue cross-reactions and notes IgM false positives from flavivirus cross-reactivity, which supports greater specificity of PRNT90; the old pipeline misread a 'no differences' result about positivity rates.

'In agreement with previous reports' that ZIKV neutralising antibodies often cross-react with dengue, West Nile and yellow fever viruses: the cited review describes exactly this cross-reactivity; the percentages are the citing study's own results.
The review describes co-circulating flaviviruses, the likelihood of multiple infections and the resulting need for specific differential diagnosis, which is the point of the sentence.
Joint citation [49, 50]: this Kenyan study shows temperature (a climatic condition) affects Aedes aegypti vector competence; vegetation is presumably carried by [49].

debatable.note: The source gives the first isolation (1947) from a sentinel rhesus macaque in the Zika Forest and isolations from Aedes africanus only after 1947; the sentence runs the mosquito into the 1947 first isolation. A small imprecision.
The source dates the first human cases to 1952 (neutralising antibodies in sera), not an isolation from humans; 'isolated ... in humans in 1952' is a common shorthand but not what the source reports.

Only the abstract (yellow fever booster response and pre-existing antibodies) was available; the study likely measured neutralising antibodies by PRNT, but nothing available supports the PRNT90-vs-IgM/IgG specificity claim. The off-topic tag is too strong.
'In agreement with a previous report': the cited study treats PRNT90 titres of 10 or more as positive; it does not discuss 1:64-1:128 titres as highly suggestive, so the agreement is loose.

A dengue/yellow fever coinfection case report that mentions cross-neutralisation of ZIKV convalescent sera with other flaviviruses; consistent with frequent cross-reactivity, but not with the specific 13.8%/86.0% split.
A mosquito vector-competence study of ZIKV/CHIKV co-infection; it reports no human prevalence, so it can neither agree nor disagree with the 39% figure. Cited in the range [41-43].

Lee et al. show virus-induced senescence with a SASP of cytokines and matrix-degrading proteases; the telomere-shortening remark is general background, not attributed to them.

debatable.note: The review supports IL-8's role in attracting neutrophils but does not mention endothelial cell migration; a partly supported list.
